title: Taxes, Costs and Pitfalls
intro: You keep what remains after fees, taxes and mistakes. These are the parts of investing you control most directly, and getting them right adds more to most people's results than any choice of stock or fund. Tax rules vary by country and change often; examples here are mainly from the United States and are illustrative, so check current rules or ask a qualified adviser.

items: Fund expenses (expense ratio) and advisory fees: a 1% advisory fee on top of fund costs is common; robo-advisers charge around 0.25%.
Trading costs: commissions (mostly zero now for US stocks and ETFs), bid-ask spreads, and market impact for larger trades.

Sales loads and commissions on some mutual funds, annuities and insurance products. Variable annuities and whole-life insurance sold as investments often carry total costs of 2 to 3% a year plus surrender charges.
Cash drag: uninvested cash in a fund or account.
Taxes: often the largest cost of all in taxable accounts.

blocks.text: Over 30 years, each 1% a year of total cost takes roughly a quarter of the ending value (see the plots in The Mathematics of Money and Funds). An adviser can still be worth paying, for planning, tax work, and above all for keeping you invested in a crash, but be clear what you are paying and for what. Prefer fiduciaries, who are legally bound to act in your interest, and fee-only advisers who aren't paid commissions on products.
How investment income is taxed (US example)

items: Interest from bonds and cash: ordinary income rates (Treasury interest exempt from state tax; most muni interest exempt from federal tax).

Qualified dividends: taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15% or 20% depending on income), if holding-period rules are met; non-qualified dividends (most REIT dividends, for example) at ordinary rates.
Capital gains: profit on a sale. Short-term (held one year or less) at ordinary rates; long-term (more than a year) at the lower rates. High earners may also owe the 3.8% net investment income tax.
Cost basis is what you paid (plus reinvested dividends); keep records, or rely on the broker's.
Losses offset gains, and up to \$3,000 a year of net losses offsets ordinary income, with the rest carried forward.
Foreign taxes withheld on foreign dividends can often be claimed as a credit in taxable accounts.
Step-up in basis: assets inherited at death currently get a basis equal to their value at death, wiping out the unrealized gain.

blocks.text: Other countries differ: the UK has annual capital gains and dividend allowances and wraps investments in ISAs and pensions; Canada taxes half of capital gains; many countries have no separate long-term rate. The principles below carry over.

items: Use tax-advantaged accounts first, starting with any employer match.
Hold for more than a year before selling winners in taxable accounts.
Prefer tax-efficient funds (broad index ETFs) in taxable accounts; put bonds and REITs in sheltered accounts (asset location).

Tax-loss harvesting: sell investments that are below cost to realize the loss, and buy a similar but not 'substantially identical' fund to stay invested. In the US the wash-sale rule disallows the loss if you buy the same security within 30 days before or after the sale.
Gain harvesting: in years with low income, realize gains at the 0% long-term rate to reset basis higher.
Give appreciated shares instead of cash to charity: no capital gains tax, and a deduction for the full value if you itemize.
Roth conversions in low-income years can reduce lifetime taxes.

Ponzi schemes pay earlier investors with new investors' money and report smooth, steady returns. Bernie Madoff's, exposed in 2008, was the largest, at roughly \$65 billion in reported (fictitious) value. His reported returns were suspiciously consistent; Harry Markopolos warned the SEC years earlier.
Pump-and-dump: promoters hype a small, thinly traded stock or token, then sell into the buying they created. Modern versions run through social media and chat groups.
Affinity fraud targets communities through trust (religious groups, ethnic communities, clubs).

Advance-fee, 'guaranteed return' and recovery scams: anyone promising high returns with no risk, pressing you to act now, or asking for payment in crypto or gift cards is almost certainly a fraud. So is someone offering to recover money you lost to a previous scam for a fee.
Crypto-specific: fake exchanges and apps, 'pig butchering' romance-investment scams, rug pulls.

blocks.text: Check that any firm or adviser is registered (in the US: FINRA BrokerCheck, the SEC's IAPD; in the UK: the FCA register). If an opportunity is so good that it must be kept secret or decided today, walk away.
The common ways investors lose money

items: Concentration: too much in one stock, often an employer's.
Leverage: margin, leveraged ETFs, options sold without understanding the tail.
Panic selling in crashes and buying back after recovery.
Chasing performance and fads.
High costs that compound silently for decades.
Not investing at all, or holding too much cash for long-term goals, losing to inflation.
Reaching for yield: buying risky high-yield products because the income looks attractive, without seeing the risk that pays for it.
Complexity: products you can't explain in two sentences (structured notes, non-traded REITs, complex insurance) are usually designed to be sold, not bought.
No emergency fund, forcing sales at bad times.

blocks.title: Short or long term
blocks.text: You are in a 32% ordinary income bracket and the 15% long-term rate. You have a \$10,000 gain on shares held 11 months. How much tax do you save by waiting another month to sell?
solution: Short-term: $0.32 \times 10000 = \$3{,}200$. Long-term: $0.15 \times 10000 = \$1{,}500$. Waiting saves \$1,700, if the price holds.

blocks.title: Tax-loss harvesting
blocks.text: You hold a total-market fund bought for \$50,000, now worth \$42,000. You sell it and immediately buy a different fund tracking a similar but different index. You realized gains of \$5,000 elsewhere this year. What is the effect?
solution: The \$8,000 loss offsets the \$5,000 gain, and \$3,000 more offsets ordinary income this year (US rules). You remain invested. Your new basis is \$42,000, so you will owe more tax later when you sell; the benefit is deferral and possibly a lower rate, not elimination. Buying the same fund within 30 days would trigger the wash-sale rule.
blocks.answer: \$8,000 loss used: \$5,000 against gains, \$3,000 against income

blocks.title: Spot the scam
blocks.text: A friend's contact offers a fund that has returned 1% every single month for six years, with no down months, run by a firm whose auditor is a tiny practice no one has heard of. What concerns would you raise?
solution: Returns that smooth are almost impossible for real investments (a 12% yearly return with near-zero volatility implies an absurd Sharpe ratio); an obscure auditor; access through personal networks (affinity). These were exactly the signs in the Madoff case. Ask for independent custody of assets and verify the registrations, or simply walk away.
blocks.answer: smooth returns, unknown auditor, affinity access
